newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: NATO pledges alliance membership door to stay open.
newsitem.headline: NATO pledges alliance membership door to stay open.

text.p: NATO, seeking avoid new divisions in Europe, pledged on Thursday to keep the alliance's doors open after it admits new members from the former communist east bloc at a summit in Madrid next month.

The ministers, gathered in the Portuguese town of Sintra to debate formally the most radical change in European security since World War Two, said they would ask their leaders to make clear enlargement was a continuing process.

"We recommend to our heads of state and government to make explicit our commitment the Alliance remains open to any other European state able and willing to fulfill the principles (of membership) and contribute to our common security," they said in a final communique.
The ministers said the July 8-9 summit in Madrid should "give substance to this commitment".

The joint communique was issued after a lunchtime discussion lasting several hours on which countries should be invited to join the West's defence club, the first time North Atlantic Treaty Organisation capitals have discussed in detail the merits of different candidates.

NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, charged with the highly sensitive task of drawing up the list of successful countries, presented a report on a round of intensive talks with all applicants and an analysis of their respective chances.

"These preparations will allow in the weeks to come the formulation of the comprehensive recommendations which we requested at our last meeting," the communique stated, NATO shorthand for saying the time for decision had arrived.
Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Slovenia, Bulgaria, Romania, Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, and the former Yugoslav Repubic of Macedonia have all applied for membership.
Solana will now start work on a shortlist of candidates and visit their respective capitals to inform them of the results.

Officials say he hopes to have a final list ready by the end of June, barely a week before the historic summit to inaugurate a new security order intended to guarantee peace in Europe in the 21st Century.
All NATO's 16 states stressed no final decisions had yet been taken, but it is well-known that former communist Warsaw pact members Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic lead the field.

Tiny Slovenia, which fulfils many of the formal conditions, and Romania, backed strongly by France and Italy, have made strong late challenges, complicating the process of how to expand the alliance without weakening it.
Fresh from negotiating a landmark security pact with Russia to run in parallel with expansion, Solana insisted only ministers attend the session.

NATO has said any former communist country wishing to be considered must have established democratic control of its armed forces, set up a market economy, and be attempting to make its forces compatible with those of the alliance.

But privately officials admit the decision on who to invite is essentially a political one and NATO capitals are desperate to avoid creating new tensions between those gaining admittance and those that do not.

Underlining this, U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and others have been at pains to insist the enlargement process would continue after Madrid, and have also agreed an enhanced partnership programme for other states.
Albright was also quoted as saying new members must meet the highest possible standards before they join and be able to contribute to NATO's common security.
"First we want to make NATO stronger and more cohesive by adding new allies who are eager and able to contribute to our common security," Albright said.

The Sintra meeting comes two days after NATO agreed a new security relationship with Moscow, effectively winning its grudging approval to at least a limited alliance expansion by setting up a permanent NATO-Russia Council at NATO headquarters.
Earlier on Thursday, the ministers also initialled a security pact with Ukraine giving the country a special status above that of partnership, but below that accorded to Russia.

The meeting also reviewed planned reforms of the alliance's command structures to allow it to carry out more varied missions and strongly criticised the former warring parties in Bosnia for failing to carry out the provisions of the Dayton peace accords.
